extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Cervantes / students of classic literature
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt (chapters 25–27) of Cervantes' Don Quixote describing the braying episode, a puppet-show, and metacommentary on performance, truthfulness, and valuation. Contains embedded evaluative remarks about shows, divination, and knightly behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braying quality (tone, timing, finish)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the tone you have got is deep, your voice is well kept up as to time and pitch, and your finishing notes come thick and fast’ — praise used to evaluate who brays best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative dimensions for a convincing bray include depth of tone, control of timing and pitch, and strong finishing notes. The passage treats these as observable, comparable skills (one brayer yields the palm to the other on these grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to text / narrative clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Go straight on with your story, and don’t run into curves and slants, for to establish a fact clearly there is need of a great deal of proof and confirmation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep to the script or main story-line; avoid digressions and needless embellishment so facts are clear and believable. The interpreter and Master Pedro repeatedly instruct the boy to ‘stick to your text’ and ‘keep to your plain song.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and avoidance of affectation in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Simplicity, boy! None of your high flights; all affectation is bad.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances should avoid over-fancy ornamentation and affected flourishes; plain, unpretentious delivery is recommended over ‘high flights’ that risk breaking the piece. (Closely linked to adherence to text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality/audience-pleasing over strict accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Are there not almost every day a thousand comedies represented all round us full of thousands of inaccuracies and absurdities, and, for all that, they have a successful run… Go on, boy, and don’t mind; for so long as I fill my pouch, no matter if I show as many inaccuracies as there are motes in a sunbeam.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers/performers may prioritise entertainment value and commercial success over factual or historical accuracy; audiences and profits can justify tolerating inaccuracies in performance. Master Pedro explicitly defends inaccuracy for the sake of earning money and attracting crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging, lighting, and explanatory showmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The show ‘set all around with lighted wax tapers which made it look splendid and bright,’ and a boy outside ‘to act as showman and explain the mysteries… having a wand in his hand to point to the figures as they came out.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual presentation (lighting, neat staging) and a clear, guiding narrator/presenter (pointing out scenes) are part of successful spectacle. Use of props, lighting, and an explicator improves audience comprehension and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation and restitution of damaged props
rubrics_metrics.description: Master Pedro names prices for destroyed figures (e.g. ‘for his death…four reals and a half’, ‘five reals and a quarter’), and appraisal is settled by arbitrators (landlord and Sancho) negotiating sums and rounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damaged theatrical property is valued according to extent of injury and replaceability; impartial arbitrators may appraise and negotiate restitution. Practical bargaining and rounding to convenient amounts are part of settling claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and credibility of divinatory performance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘this little beast gives no answer as to the future; of things past he knows something, and more or less of things present… though he does not always hit the truth in every case, most times he is not far wrong’ and Don Quixote suspects a ‘pact… with the devil.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divinatory acts are presented with explicit scope limits (past/present > future) and with measured reliability — sometimes near the truth, sometimes mistaken. Viewers/clients are urged to be skeptical, and performers may claim supernatural explanation (or be suspected of fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/historical accuracy as an evaluative point
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Quixote corrects the puppeteer: ‘bells are not in use among the Moors; only kettledrums, and a kind of small trumpet somewhat like our clarion; to ring bells this way in Sansueña is unquestionably a great absurdity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations that ignore known cultural or historical facts invite criticism from informed spectators. While some performers dismiss such trifles, accuracy can be a legitimate criterion for judgement by certain audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial/chronicler truthfulness and narrative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Cide Hamete’s opening: ‘I swear as a Catholic Christian;’ the translator comments this functions as an assertion that the chronicler ‘was telling the truth… in all he chose to write about Quixote.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chronicle or narrator may assert truthfulness to establish authority; such oaths or claimed fidelity signal an expectation that the account aims to be trustworthy (even if the text later plays with that reliability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over words as a standard for knighthood/performance (‘operibus credite et non verbis’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Master Pedro’s motto ‘operibus credite et non verbis’ and Don Quixote’s behaviour — ‘suiting the action to the word’ by attacking the puppet-Moors to defend the lovers — underscore a principle that deeds validate claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether assessing a performer, chronicler, or knight-errant, actions (tangible deeds, effective performance) are treated as the real test of merit rather than mere verbal claims. This is offered both as theatrical advice and as a moral/behavioral standard.
